title: Hands-on Exercise 1: A Layered Grammar of Graphics
text:
3. The Grammar of Graphics
ggplot2 builds every plot from seven layered components. Understanding these components is essential to constructing meaningful visualisations.







Component
Role




Data
The dataset being plotted


Aesthetics
Maps data variables to visual properties (position, colour, size, shape)


Geometrics
The visual marks used to represent data (points, bars, lines)


Facets
Splits data into subplots by a categorical variable


Statistics
Applies statistical transformations (mean, confidence intervals)


Coordinates
Defines the plane on which data is mapped


Themes
Controls non-data elements such as background and fonts



A plot is built by stacking these layers using the + operator.

title: Hands-on Exercise 1: A Layered Grammar of Graphics
text:
4. Base R Graphics vs ggplot2
To appreciate the advantages of ggplot2, it is useful to compare it with Base R graphics using the same dataset.

Show code
# Base R
hist(exam_data$MATHS,
     main = "Distribution of Maths Scores",
     xlab = "Maths Score",
     col = "grey80")
# ggplot2
ggplot(exam_data, aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20,
                 fill = "steelblue",
                 color = "white") +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Maths Scores",
       x = "Maths Score",
       y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal()







Base R: hist()







ggplot2: geom_histogram()





While Base R offers a quick way to produce plots, ggplot2 provides a more systematic and extensible framework, especially when dealing with complex multi-layered visualisations.

title: Hands-on Exercise 1: A Layered Grammar of Graphics
text:
5. Essential Geometric Objects
Geometric objects (geoms) define what type of mark is drawn on the plot. Below are the key geoms introduced in this exercise.

5.1 Bar Chart — geom_bar()
Used to visualise the frequency of a categorical variable.


Show code
ggplot(exam_data, aes(x = RACE)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "steelblue") +
  labs(title = "Number of Students by Race",
       x = "Race", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal()











5.2 Dot Plot — geom_dotplot()
Each dot represents one observation. Useful for small datasets to see individual data points.


Show code
ggplot(exam_data, aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_dotplot(binwidth = 2.5,
               dotsize = 0.5,
               fill = "steelblue") +
  scale_y_continuous(NULL, breaks = NULL) +
  labs(title = "Dot Plot of Maths Scores",
       x = "Maths Score") +
  theme_minimal()















Note



The y-axis is suppressed here as it does not carry meaningful information in a dot plot.




5.3 Histogram — geom_histogram()
Used to visualise the distribution of a continuous variable.

Show code
ggplot(exam_data, aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20,
                 fill = "steelblue",
                 color = "white") +
  labs(title = "Maths Score Distribution",
       x = "Maths Score", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal()
ggplot(exam_data, aes(x = MATHS, fill = GENDER)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20,
                 color = "grey30") +
  labs(title = "Maths Score Distribution by Gender",
       x = "Maths Score", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal()







Default histogram







Coloured by gender







5.4 Kernel Density Plot — geom_density()
A smoothed version of the histogram, useful for visualising the underlying distribution.


Show code
ggplot(exam_data, aes(x = MATHS, colour = GENDER)) +
  geom_density(linewidth = 0.8) +
  labs(title = "Kernel Density Estimate of Maths Scores by Gender",
       x = "Maths Score", y = "Density") +
  theme_minimal()











5.5 Boxplot — geom_boxplot()
Displays the five-number summary (minimum, Q1, median, Q3, maximum) and highlights outliers.

Show code
ggplot(exam_data, aes(x = GENDER, y = MATHS)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.6) +
  labs(title = "Maths Scores by Gender",
       x = "Gender", y = "Maths Score") +
  theme_minimal()
ggplot(exam_data, aes(x = GENDER, y = MATHS)) +
  geom_boxplot(notch = TRUE,
               fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.6) +
  labs(title = "Notched Boxplot of Maths Scores by Gender",
       x = "Gender", y = "Maths Score") +
  theme_minimal()







Standard boxplot







Notched boxplot











Tip



If the notches of two boxplots do not overlap, there is strong evidence that their medians differ.




5.6 Violin Plot — geom_violin()
Combines a boxplot with a kernel density estimate, showing both summary statistics and the full distribution shape.


Show code
ggplot(exam_data, aes(x = GENDER, y = MATHS)) +
  geom_violin(fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.6) +
  labs(title = "Violin Plot of Maths Scores by Gender",
       x = "Gender", y = "Maths Score") +
  theme_minimal()











5.7 Scatterplot — geom_point()
Used to visualise the relationship between two continuous variables.


Show code
ggplot(exam_data, aes(x = MATHS, y = ENGLISH)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, colour = "steelblue") +
  labs(title = "Maths vs English Scores",
       x = "Maths Score", y = "English Score") +
  theme_minimal()











5.8 Combining Geoms
Multiple geoms can be layered on the same plot using +.


Show code
ggplot(exam_data, aes(x = GENDER, y = MATHS)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_point(position = "jitter",

7. Facets
Facets generate small multiples — the same plot repeated across subsets of data. This is particularly useful for comparing distributions across groups.

7.1 facet_wrap()
Wraps panels into a 2D grid, ideal for a single grouping variable.


Show code
ggplot(exam_data, aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20,
                 fill = "steelblue",
                 color = "white") +
  facet_wrap(~ CLASS) +
  labs(title = "Maths Score Distribution by Class",
       x = "Maths Score", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal()











7.2 facet_grid()
Forms a matrix of panels defined by two grouping variables.


Show code

  geom_histogram(bins = 20,
                 fill = "steelblue",
                 color = "white") +
  facet_grid(~ CLASS) +

title: Hands-on Exercise 1: A Layered Grammar of Graphics
text:
10. Key Takeaways
This exercise demonstrates that ggplot2’s layered grammar provides a principled and flexible framework for building statistical graphics. The key insights are:

Start with data and aesthetics — define what variables map to which visual properties
Choose the right geom — different geoms suit different data types and analytical goals
Layer deliberately — combining geoms (e.g. boxplot + jitter) reveals more information than either alone
Use facets for comparison — small multiples are more effective than overloaded single plots
Apply statistical summaries — overlaying means or trend lines adds analytical value
Fix axis ranges — always set equal axis limits when comparing two variables on the same scale
Choose themes purposefully — theme_minimal() or theme_classic() are generally preferred for clean, publication-ready visuals

3. Beyond ggplot2 Annotation: ggrepel
When plotting a scatterplot with many data points, adding labels using geom_label() or geom_text() often results in overlapping text that is difficult to read.

3.1 The Problem: Overlapping Labels


Show code
ggplot(exam_data,
       aes(x = MATHS, y = ENGLISH)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = lm, linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_label(aes(label = ID),
             hjust = 0.5,
             vjust = -0.5) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 100),
                  ylim = c(0, 100)) +
  labs(title = "English scores versus Maths scores for Primary 3",
       x = "Maths Score", y = "English Score") +
  theme_minimal()











3.2 The Solution: ggrepel
ggrepel solves this by automatically adjusting label positions to avoid overlap. Simply replace:

geom_label() → geom_label_repel()
geom_text() → geom_text_repel()



Show code
ggplot(exam_data,
       aes(x = MATHS, y = ENGLISH)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = lm, linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_label_repel(aes(label = ID),
                   fontface = "bold",
                   max.overlaps = 20) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 100),
                  ylim = c(0, 100)) +
  labs(title = "English scores versus Maths scores for Primary 3",
       x = "Maths Score", y = "English Score") +
  theme_minimal()

text:
5. Beyond Single Graph: patchwork
In data storytelling, a single chart is rarely sufficient. patchwork allows us to combine multiple ggplot2 plots into one cohesive composite figure using simple, intuitive operators.

5.1 Creating the Individual Plots
We first create three plots separately and store them as objects:


Show code
p1 <- ggplot(exam_data, aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20,
                 boundary = 100,
                 color = "grey25",
                 fill = "grey90") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 100)) +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Maths Scores") +
  theme_minimal()

p2 <- ggplot(exam_data, aes(x = ENGLISH)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20,
                 boundary = 100,
                 color = "grey25",
                 fill = "grey90") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 100)) +
  labs(title = "Distribution of English Scores") +
  theme_minimal()

p3 <- ggplot(exam_data,
             aes(x = MATHS, y = ENGLISH)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(method = lm, linewidth = 0.5) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 100),
                  ylim = c(0, 100)) +
  labs(title = "English vs Maths Scores",
       x = "Maths Score", y = "English Score") +
  theme_minimal()




5.2 Two-Column Layout: +
The + operator places two plots side by side:


Show code
p1 + p2











5.3 Three-Plot Composite Layout
Using a combination of / (stack vertically) and | (place side by side):


Show code
(p1 / p2) | p3











5.4 Adding Tags to Subplots
plot_annotation() automatically labels each subplot, making it easy to reference them in text:


Show code
((p1 / p2) | p3) +
  plot_annotation(tag_levels = "I")











5.5 Inset Plot
inset_element() allows you to embed a smaller plot inside a larger one, useful for showing a zoomed-in view or a supplementary chart:


Show code
p3 + inset_element(p2,
                   left = 0.02,
                   bottom = 0.7,
                   right = 0.5,
                   top = 1)











5.6 Combining patchwork with ggthemes
The & operator applies a theme to all plots in a patchwork composite simultaneously:


Show code
patchwork <- (p1 / p2) | p3
patchwork & theme_economist()















Note



Notice the difference between + and & in patchwork:

+ adds elements to the last plot only
& applies the element to all plots in the composite

title: Hands-on Exercise 4: Seeing Distributions, Quantifying Uncertainty, Embedding Statistics, and Comparing Fairly
text:
This exercise covers four seemingly independent topics: visualising distributions, visualising uncertainty, visual statistical analysis, and funnel plots for fair comparison. At first I thought they had nothing to do with each other, but after working through them I realised they form a complete progression in how seriously we take a chart.
I reorganised the order based on my own understanding:
Step one, use ridgeline and raincloud plots to see the shape of the data clearly. This is the starting point of any analysis.
Step two, recognise that the sample mean is not the true mean. So we use error bars and ggdist to draw out how confident we actually are.
Step three, take it further by embedding the results of statistical tests (p values, effect sizes, Bayes factors) directly into the chart, so a single image performs both exploration and inference.
Step four, apply everything we have learned to a real problem: when sample sizes vary widely across entities (hospitals, schools, regions), how do we make a fair side-by-side comparison? That is what funnel plots are for.
By the end I realised these four chapters are not really four tools. They are a complete chain of thinking: from looking, to inferring, to comparing.

section: 2.1 Ridgeline Plot: Best Choice When You Have Many Groups
text:
2.1 Ridgeline Plot: Best Choice When You Have Many Groups
The essence of a ridgeline plot is stacking multiple distributions vertically with slight overlap, so you can compare many groups in a compact space.
Only consider it when you have 5 or more groups. With fewer groups, faceted density plots work better. Our CLASS variable has 9 classes, which is in the sweet spot.

2.1.1 Basic Ridgeline

ggplot(exam, 
       aes(x = ENGLISH, 
           y = CLASS)) +
  geom_density_ridges(
    scale = 3,
    rel_min_height = 0.01,
    bandwidth = 3.4,
    fill = lighten("#7097BB", .3),
    color = "white"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    name = "English Grades",
    expand = c(0, 0)
  ) +
  scale_y_discrete(name = NULL, 
                   expand = expansion(add = c(0.2, 2.6))) +
  theme_ridges()








How I think about the key parameters:
scale = 3 controls the height of each ridge. The larger the value, the chunkier the ridge and the more they overlap. I tried 1 and 5 and found 3 hits the sweet spot between “I can still see the shape of each ridge” and “the whole thing looks compact”.
rel_min_height = 0.01 cuts off the very low density tails. Without it you get long thin tails that are barely visible but still take up space.
bandwidth = 3.4 is the kernel density bandwidth. A small bandwidth gives a jagged curve, and a large one over-smooths and hides real structure.


2.1.2 Mapping Probability Information onto Color
Next level move: let the color carry information. The version below uses the empirical cumulative distribution function (ECDF) to compute the tail probability at each x position. The closer to the extremes, the darker the color.

ggplot(exam,
       aes(x = ENGLISH, 
           y = CLASS, 
           fill = 0.5 - abs(0.5 - after_stat(ecdf)))) +
  stat_density_ridges(geom = "density_ridges_gradient", 
                      calc_ecdf = TRUE) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Tail probability",
                       direction = -1) +
  theme_ridges()








A regular ridgeline only tells me what the distribution looks like for this class. The tail probability version tells me where any individual student sits within their own class. The dark areas are the extreme values (very high or very low) for that class.
Note that calc_ecdf = TRUE must be turned on, otherwise after_stat(ecdf) has no value to access. I forgot this the first time and spent a while debugging the error.


2.1.3 Coloring by Quartile
Another approach is to slice the distribution into quartiles and color each slice differently:

ggplot(exam,
       aes(x = ENGLISH, 
           y = CLASS, 
           fill = factor(after_stat(quantile)))) +
  stat_density_ridges(
    geom = "density_ridges_gradient",
    calc_ecdf = TRUE, 
    quantiles = 4,
    quantile_lines = TRUE) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(name = "Quartiles") +
  theme_ridges()








The biggest advantage of this version is that the median line is immediately visible (the boundary between the two middle slices). For “quickly comparing the central location across many groups”, this version beats the ECDF one.

title: Hands-on Exercise 4: Seeing Distributions, Quantifying Uncertainty, Embedding Statistics, and Comparing Fairly
section: 2.2 Raincloud Plot: Combining Boxplot, Density, and Dotplot in One
text:
2.2 Raincloud Plot: Combining Boxplot, Density, and Dotplot in One
Raincloud is named that way because it has three layers: the “cloud” on top (a half density), the “rain” in the middle (a boxplot), and the “rain drops” at the bottom (a dotplot). Three perspectives at once, each compensating for the others’ blind spots.

2.2.1 Layer One: Half-Eye

ggplot(exam, 
       aes(x = RACE, 
           y = ENGLISH)) +
  stat_halfeye(adjust = 0.5,
               justification = -0.2,
               .width = 0,
               point_colour = NA)








justification = -0.2 shifts the half density slightly to the right, leaving room for the boxplot we will add next. .width = 0 and point_colour = NA turn off the default “point + interval” decoration that ggdist adds by default, because at this layer I only want the density shape.


2.2.2 Layer Two: Boxplot

ggplot(exam, 
       aes(x = RACE, 
           y = ENGLISH)) +
  stat_halfeye(adjust = 0.5,
               justification = -0.2,
               .width = 0,
               point_colour = NA) +
  geom_boxplot(width = .20,
               outlier.shape = NA)








width = .20 squeezes the boxplot into a thin “needle” so it does not steal visual focus from the density. outlier.shape = NA hides the outliers, because the upcoming dotplot will draw all individual points anyway, so duplicate outlier marks are unnecessary.


2.2.3 Layer Three: Dotplot

ggplot(exam, 
       aes(x = RACE, 
           y = ENGLISH)) +
  stat_halfeye(adjust = 0.5,
               justification = -0.2,
               .width = 0,
               point_colour = NA) +
  geom_boxplot(width = .20,
               outlier.shape = NA) +
  stat_dots(side = "left", 
            justification = 1.2, 
            binwidth = NA,
            dotsize = 2)








side = "left" puts the dots on the left side, mirroring the density on the right. justification = 1.2 pushes them further left to avoid overlapping with the boxplot.


2.2.4 Final Polished Version
Flip the coordinates and apply a clean theme to get the classic horizontal raincloud:

ggplot(exam, 
       aes(x = RACE, 
           y = ENGLISH)) +
  stat_halfeye(adjust = 0.5,
               justification = -0.2,
               .width = 0,
               point_colour = NA) +
  geom_boxplot(width = .20,
               outlier.shape = NA) +
  stat_dots(side = "left", 
            justification = 1.2, 
            binwidth = NA,
            dotsize = 1.5) +
  coord_flip() +
  theme_economist()

3.1 Manually Drawing Error Bars with ggplot2
The classic approach. First use dplyr to compute the mean, standard deviation, and standard error for each group:

my_sum <- exam %>%
  group_by(RACE) %>%
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean = mean(MATHS),
    sd = sd(MATHS)
  ) %>%
  mutate(se = sd / sqrt(n - 1))

knitr::kable(my_sum, format = 'html')

How I think about these statistics: standard deviation (sd) describes how spread out the data itself is. Standard error (se) describes how uncertain we are about the mean estimate. These two are often confused. The formula for se is sd divided by sqrt(n), which means the larger the sample, the more precise our estimate of the mean, and the smaller the se.

3.1.1 Standard Error Bars

ggplot(my_sum) +
  geom_errorbar(
    aes(x = RACE, 
        ymin = mean - se, 
        ymax = mean + se), 
    width = 0.2, 
    colour = "black", 
    alpha = 0.9, 
    linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_point(aes(x = RACE, 
                 y = mean), 
             stat = "identity", 
             color = "red",
             size = 1.5,
             alpha = 1) +
  ggtitle("Standard Error of Mean Maths Score by Race")










3.1.2 95% Confidence Intervals
Replace ±1 SE with ±1.96 SE to get the 95% confidence interval. I also added reorder() to sort by mean, which makes the chart easier to read:

ggplot(my_sum) +
  geom_errorbar(
    aes(x = reorder(RACE, -mean), 
        ymin = mean - 1.96*se, 
        ymax = mean + 1.96*se), 
    width = 0.2, 
    colour = "black", 
    alpha = 0.9, 
    linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_point(aes(x = RACE, 
                 y = mean), 
             stat = "identity", 
             color = "red",
             size = 1.5,
             alpha = 1) +
  labs(x = "Race",
       y = "Mean Maths Score",
       title = "95% Confidence Interval of Mean Maths Score by Race")








The trick to reading this chart: if two groups’ confidence intervals do not overlap, their means are almost certainly significantly different; if they overlap heavily, the difference is likely not significant. This is a much smarter visual judgement than just eyeballing bar heights.

text:
3.2 Doing It Elegantly with ggdist
The ggdist package offers a much cleaner syntax. No need to compute summaries manually.

3.2.1 stat_pointinterval: Auto-Compute Intervals

exam %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = RACE, y = MATHS)) +
  stat_pointinterval() +
  labs(
    title = "Multiple Confidence Intervals of Mean Maths Score",
    subtitle = "Default shows 66% and 95% intervals")








ggdist by default draws two layers of lines with different thicknesses, representing the 66% and 95% intervals. This multiple intervals in one chart design carries more information than a single interval.


3.2.2 Customising the Intervals
If we only want the 95% interval and switch the point to median:

exam %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = RACE, y = MATHS)) +
  stat_pointinterval(.width = 0.95,
                     .point = median,
                     .interval = qi) +
  labs(
    title = "95% Interval of Median Maths Score",
    subtitle = "Median is more robust to outliers than mean")








I noticed that ggdist treats mean and median as first-class citizens equally. When the data is skewed or has outliers, median is more reliable than mean. Being able to swap so easily is a big advantage of ggdist.


3.2.3 Showing Multiple Confidence Levels at Once

exam %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = RACE, y = MATHS)) +
  stat_pointinterval(
    .width = c(0.95, 0.99),
    show.legend = FALSE) +
  labs(
    title = "Showing 95% and 99% Intervals Simultaneously",
    subtitle = "Outer thick line = 95%, inner thin line = 99%")










3.2.4 Gradient Interval Plot (Prettier and More Honest)

exam %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = RACE, y = MATHS)) +
  stat_gradientinterval(   
    fill = "skyblue",      
    show.legend = TRUE     
  ) +                        
  labs(
    title = "Gradient-Style Uncertainty Visualisation",
    subtitle = "Darker areas indicate higher probability of the estimate")








Why I think this gradient design is great: it removes the binary “inside vs outside the interval” split. Traditional error bars make people feel “every value inside the interval is equally likely”, but the truth is that values closer to the center are more likely. The gradient version is more honest about that.

3.3 Wrap-up of Part 2
Core idea of uncertainty visualisation: every point estimate should come with its uncertainty information. Otherwise we are deceiving the reader.
Manual error bars give precise control over every detail and are great for publication-ready charts. ggdist’s one-liner is better for exploratory analysis. I will keep both tools in my toolkit and pick based on the situation.

title: Hands-on Exercise 4: Seeing Distributions, Quantifying Uncertainty, Embedding Statistics, and Comparing Fairly
text:
4.1 One-Sample Test: gghistostats
Suppose we want to test whether the mean English score across all students equals 60. The traditional workflow is to run a t-test, then draw a histogram, then verbally explain the result. gghistostats collapses all three into one:

set.seed(1234)

gghistostats(
  data = exam,
  x = ENGLISH,
  type = "bayes",
  test.value = 60,
  xlab = "English Scores"
)








The information density in the title area is enormous. What appears here is BF₁₀, the Bayes factor. It tells us the strength of evidence in favor of the alternative hypothesis relative to the strength of evidence in favor of the null.
My quick reference for interpreting Bayes factors (based on Jeffreys 1961, revised by Lee & Wagenmakers 2013):



BF₁₀ Range
Interpretation




> 100
Extreme evidence for H₁


30 to 100
Very strong evidence for H₁


10 to 30
Strong evidence for H₁


3 to 10
Moderate evidence for H₁


1 to 3
Anecdotal evidence for H₁


1
No evidence for either


1/3 to 1
Anecdotal evidence for H₀


1/10 to 1/3
Moderate evidence for H₀



The advantage of Bayes factors over p values: they are symmetric. They can quantify both “evidence for H₀” and “evidence for H₁”, whereas p values can only reject H₀ but cannot “accept H₀”.

Comparing maths scores between male and female students:

ggbetweenstats(
  data = exam,
  x = GENDER, 
  y = MATHS,
  type = "np",
  messages = FALSE

4.3 One-Way ANOVA: Still ggbetweenstats
Switch the grouping variable from binary to multi-class (RACE), and add pairwise comparisons:

ggbetweenstats(
  data = exam,
  x = RACE, 
  y = ENGLISH,
  type = "p",
  mean.ci = TRUE, 
  pairwise.comparisons = TRUE, 
  pairwise.display = "s",
  p.adjust.method = "fdr",
  messages = FALSE
)








Parameter notes (these are things I had to dig into the docs to figure out):
pairwise.display = "s" only shows pairwise comparisons that are statistically significant, avoiding a chart cluttered with “ns” (not significant) labels.
p.adjust.method = "fdr" uses the False Discovery Rate method to correct p values for multiple comparisons. Not correcting for multiple comparisons inflates the false positive rate dramatically. FDR is one of the most popular correction methods today.

exam1 <- exam %>%

section: 5.4 Building One from Scratch with ggplot2
text:
5.4 Building One from Scratch with ggplot2
The best way to understand the principle of a funnel plot is to build one by hand. Step one, compute the rate and standard error for each point:

df <- covid19 %>%
  mutate(rate = Death / Positive) %>%
  mutate(rate.se = sqrt((rate * (1 - rate)) / Positive)) %>%
  filter(rate > 0)

rate.se uses the binomial standard error formula sqrt(p(1-p)/n). This formula is crucial. It explains why the funnel narrows as n grows: larger n means larger denominator, smaller se, and a tighter “reasonable range”.
Step two, compute the overall weighted average rate across all entities, used as the funnel’s centerline:

fit.mean <- weighted.mean(df$rate, 1 / df$rate.se^2)
fit.mean

[1] 0.01496959


Notice the weight is 1/se^2, which is inverse-variance weighting. This is the standard practice in meta-analysis. The idea is “the more precise the estimate, the higher its weight”.
Step three, generate the upper and lower bound curves for 95% and 99.9%:

number.seq <- seq(1, max(df$Positive), 1)
number.ll95 <- fit.mean - 1.96 * sqrt((fit.mean*(1-fit.mean)) / number.seq) 
number.ul95 <- fit.mean + 1.96 * sqrt((fit.mean*(1-fit.mean)) / number.seq) 
number.ll999 <- fit.mean - 3.29 * sqrt((fit.mean*(1-fit.mean)) / number.seq) 
number.ul999 <- fit.mean + 3.29 * sqrt((fit.mean*(1-fit.mean)) / number.seq) 

dfCI <- data.frame(number.ll95, number.ul95, number.ll999, 
                   number.ul999, number.seq, fit.mean)

1.96 corresponds to two-sided 95%, and 3.29 corresponds to two-sided 99.8% (also known as the 3 sigma rule).
Step four, draw the chart:

p <- ggplot(df, aes(x = Positive, y = rate)) +
  geom_point(aes(label = `Sub-district`), 
             alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_line(data = dfCI, 
            aes(x = number.seq, y = number.ll95), 
            size = 0.4, colour = "grey40", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(data = dfCI, 
            aes(x = number.seq, y = number.ul95), 
            size = 0.4, colour = "grey40", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(data = dfCI, 
            aes(x = number.seq, y = number.ll999), 
            size = 0.4, colour = "grey40") +
  geom_line(data = dfCI, 
            aes(x = number.seq, y = number.ul999), 
            size = 0.4, colour = "grey40") +
  geom_hline(data = dfCI, 
             aes(yintercept = fit.mean), 
             size = 0.4, colour = "grey40") +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 0.05)) +
  annotate("text", x = 1, y = -0.13, label = "95%", size = 3, colour = "grey40") + 
  annotate("text", x = 4.5, y = -0.18, label = "99%", size = 3, colour = "grey40") + 
  ggtitle("Cumulative Fatality Rate by Cumulative Number of COVID-19 Cases") +
  xlab("Cumulative Number of COVID-19 Cases") + 
  ylab("Cumulative Fatality Rate") +
  theme_light() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 12),
        legend.position = c(0.91, 0.85), 
        legend.title = element_text(size = 7),
        legend.text = element_text(size = 7),
        legend.background = element_rect(colour = "grey60", linetype = "dotted"),
        legend.key.height = unit(0.3, "cm"))
p

text:
5.6 Wrap-up of Part 4
Funnel plots taught me one thing: “fair comparison” is always more important than “direct comparison”.
The media often produces these rankings: “national hospital death rate ranking”, “national school admission rate ranking”. Without considering sample size, almost all such rankings are misleading. Funnel plots give us a standard method to ask: is this difference real, or is it just random fluctuation caused by sample size?

The deck has five parts. Part one is setup. I look at the marginal distribution of each variable before any cross-comparisons, so I know what I’m working with. Part two is the profitability side, where loss ratio is the main metric and every visual is paired with a statistical test. title: Insurance PortfolioProfitability & Volatility
text:
Setting the Scene

“Insurers often carry underperforming portfolios where the root causes of poor profitability and high volatility are unknown.”



354,091 Policy-years


70.3% Portfolio Loss Ratio


2022 to 2024 Observation window


47 Variables


The remediation question. A portfolio Loss Ratio of 70.3% looks fine on average, but averages hide a lot of leakage. I want to know where the LR is mis-distributed across product, driver, vehicle and time, and how unstable each pocket is. Both questions get answered visually first, then validated with statistics.

The quote at the top sums up the problem. Bad books rarely fail because there is no signal in the data. They fail because the signal is scattered across many variables, and no single dashboard pulls it together. The four KPI cards are the numbers I keep coming back to. The portfolio loss ratio sits around 70 percent, which on its own sounds okay. Most insurers aim for a combined ratio under 95 percent, and loss is the biggest part of that. But the word “average” is doing a lot of work. The same 70 percent can come from a stable book that bounces between 60 and 80, or a volatile one where most policies claim nothing but the top one percent eats ten times its premium. Telling those two worlds apart is the job of this study.

title: Insurance PortfolioProfitability & Volatility
text:
The Data and Analytical Sandbox


Source. Real-world Spanish motor-insurance dataset, Mendeley Data (link).
Scale. 354,091 policy-year records over 3 calendar years.
Variable families (47 in total)

Policy and insured: 8
Driver and vehicle: 10
Premiums: 8
Claim counts: 10
Incurred losses: 10
Exposure: 2

Derived KPIs. loss_ratio, pure_premium, claim_frequency, severity, a large_loss flag, plus six banded continuous variables for stratified analysis.










Figure 1








The dataset comes from Mendeley Data, published by a Spanish non-life insurer. After importing the semicolon-delimited file and fixing one cookbook inconsistency (the field labelled “age driving licence” is actually years held, which matters for any age-based pricing logic), the sandbox lands at 354,091 policy-year records over three calendar years. Missingness is small across all 47 variables, and only 49 inactive shells had to be dropped. The derived KPIs follow standard actuarial practice. Loss Ratio is the headline profitability metric, pure premium is loss per unit exposure, and a large-loss flag is set at the 99th percentile of non-zero incurred. The workflow on the right shows where each later slide sits. Univariate EDA feeds the bivariate validation, which splits into profitability and volatility tracks, and both feed the interactive layer.

title: Insurance PortfolioProfitability & Volatility
text:
Univariate Landscape, Numerical Drivers


Figure 2


Three shape diagnostics that frame later choices

driver_age is roughly Gaussian with a mean around 49. There is no young-driver hump, which probably means the insurer already screens out new licensees in volume.
vehicle_age is bimodal with a long right tail past 50 years. Spain has a real vintage-vehicle subculture and it is built into this book.
total_premium and vehicle_value are log-normal, so later LR analyses need log-scale axes or portfolio-weighted ratios. Raw arithmetic means would be dominated by tiny-premium policies.



Why histogram plus density together?
The histogram fixes the eye on observed mass. The density overlay in accent red shows the continuous shape without binning artefacts. When they disagree, for example the spike at exactly zero for total_premium, there is usually a data-quality boundary worth a closer look.



Univariate analysis is the discipline of asking what each variable looks like on its own, before correlating it with anything else. Skipping this step is a common mistake, because every later bivariate finding is conditioned on the marginal shape of its inputs. Three takeaways drive my downstream choices. First, the absence of a young-driver mass tells me the insurer is not writing 18 to 25 year-olds in volume, so the classical U-shape in age and claims may just not be observable here. Second, vehicle_age is bimodal, meaning there are basically two books inside this book, a modern fleet and a vintage fleet, and they deserve separate treatment. Third, the right-skew in financial variables means I should avoid arithmetic-mean LRs at policy level, so portfolio-weighted ratios are used for all headline figures.

title: Insurance PortfolioProfitability & Volatility
text:
Univariate Landscape, Categorical Drivers


Figure 3
Three severe class imbalances to remember in every bivariate test that follows.
bonus_score is 96.5% Good. policy_status is 89.2% Active. business_type is 69.3% New Business. And the most consequential surprise: COMP-N is only 4.6% of the book, but as I show later it is the single largest profitability risk.

Pareto-ordering the bars by frequency turns a dull frequency table into a concentration story. Three imbalances stand out. The bonus-malus system is basically a single-class system. 96.5 percent of policy-years sit in Good, so any LR difference seen between Neutral and Bad cannot rely on volume alone, and needs formal testing. Policy status at 89.2 percent Active is normal for a steady-state book. The interesting eleven percent is the Cancelled cohort, which I show later carries a 128 percent LR. The one that matters most for this study is the policy-type distribution. CC dominates at 57.8 percent. COMP-N, the no-excess comprehensive cover, is only 4.6 percent of policy-years, yet it turns out to be the single biggest profitability problem in this book. Small does not mean safe.

title: Insurance PortfolioProfitability & Volatility
text:
Profitability. LR by Categorical Drivers










Figure 4







Four findings stand out

policy_type spans 39 pp. TP basic at 54% vs. COMP-N at 94%. The single largest lever for any remediation.
The bonus-malus signal is leaking. LR is non-monotonic: Good 70%, then Bad 79%, then Neutral 81%. The “Neutral” pool looks like a dumping ground for borderline risks the system cannot cleanly classify.
Cancelled policies bleed money. 128% LR against 64% Active. This looks like adverse retention, where claimants disproportionately exit the book and leave losses behind.
Diesel runs 9 pp hotter than gasoline. A pricing or selection gap worth a re-rate study. The next slide validates it statistically.




This is probably the most information-dense slide in the deck. Six categorical drivers, all on the same Loss Ratio axis, all benchmarked against the dashed portfolio average. The colour code is direct. Red bars are worse than the book, green bars are better. Four findings deserve attention. First, product mix dominates everything else. The 39-point spread between TP and COMP-N is more than twice as wide as any other driver. Second, the bonus-malus result is the most diagnostically interesting because it is non-monotonic. Neutral is worse than Bad, which suggests Neutral is absorbing risks that should have been classified as Bad. Third, the cancellation finding hints at adverse retention. The policyholders who cancel are disproportionately the ones who have claimed. Fourth, the 9-point diesel gap is statistically robust because of the sample size on each side.

title: Insurance PortfolioProfitability & Volatility
text:
Profitability. Statistical Validation


Figure 5
Reading the test. Kruskal-Wallis confirms a highly significant between-group difference (p ≪ 0.001). Pairwise post-hoc Dunn’s tests (only significant pairs displayed) verify that every policy-type pair separates, so the headline ordering on the previous slide is not just a sample-size artefact.

A bar chart showing a 39-point Loss Ratio spread is not meaningful unless I know whether the gap is larger than what randomness would produce. The non-parametric Kruskal-Wallis test, embedded directly into the plot title by ggstatsplot, gives that audit trail. I picked non-parametric on purpose. Policy-level LR is heavily zero-inflated, because most policies have no claims, and it is right-skewed in the tail, which breaks the assumptions of a one-way ANOVA. The post-hoc Dunn pairwise tests, with only significant connections shown, confirm that every adjacent policy-type pair separates at the 0.001 level. This is the kind of visual that pairs the effect with the test in one place, which makes the result easier to defend.

section: Profitability. Continuous Drivers and Vehicle Heatmap
text:
Profitability. Continuous Drivers and Vehicle Heatmap










Figure 6





The missing U-shape is a quiet success. A flat 67% to 73% LR across all bands means the rating engine is already loading young and old drivers correctly. Age is not where remediation lives.










Figure 7





Risk concentrates in the upper-left: new, expensive vehicles. The interaction is non-linear and explains why a one-dimensional vehicle-age tariff under-prices the modern luxury segment.



Two contrasting continuous-driver stories side by side. The driver-age plot on the left is a negative finding worth celebrating. Actuarial conventional wisdom predicts a U-shape, where the youngest and oldest drivers carry the highest Loss Ratios. Instead, the profile is pretty flat, sitting between 67 and 73 percent across all bands. This is not evidence that age does not matter. It is evidence that the existing premium-rating engine is already loading age correctly, and the signal has been absorbed by the price. On the right, the two-way interaction between vehicle age and vehicle value is where there is still mispricing. The upper-left cell, new and expensive vehicles, sits well above the diagonal. A one-dimensional vehicle-age load cannot capture this interaction, and the rating table needs a value-age cross term.

title: Insurance PortfolioProfitability & Volatility
text:
Volatility. The Tail-Risk Machine










Figure 8







Gini = 0.956
A Gini of 0.95 is very high by P&C standards. A typical auto book sits between 0.85 and 0.92. In plain language, the volatility of this portfolio is basically the volatility of a few hundred policies.
What this means for the playbook

Blanket re-rating cannot fix what the tail is doing.
The only practical tools are excess-of-loss reinsurance and per-risk underwriting limits, targeted at the upper percentile.

The deterioration in average LR is a body-of-book problem. The volatility of the book is a tail problem. Confusing the two leads to the wrong remediation.



The Lorenz curve is a clean way to show tail concentration. Each point on the x-axis is a cumulative share of policies, sorted from cheapest claim to most expensive. The y-axis is the cumulative share of losses they account for. A diagonal line means perfect equality, and a sharp bow towards the bottom-right means a tiny minority drives most of the loss. The shaded area between the diagonal and the curve quantifies that inequality as the Gini coefficient. At 0.95, this book is well above the 0.85 to 0.92 range typical of a stable motor portfolio. The strategic point here is simple. Blanket re-rating cannot reduce volatility of this magnitude, because the volatility is driven by a few hundred policies that are statistically unforecastable from the body of the book. Only reinsurance and underwriting limits can manage it.

title: Insurance PortfolioProfitability & Volatility
text:
Volatility. Frequency vs. Severity Quadrant


Figure 9
Reading the quadrant. Upper-right is “double trouble”. COMP-N is the only type that claims more often and costs more per claim. TP basic sits in the opposite corner, the safe pocket. CC combined is the volume leader (biggest bubble) and anchors the portfolio’s centre of gravity.

The frequency and severity decomposition is the classical actuarial diagnostic, and putting it on a quadrant chart locates each policy type in a two-dimensional risk space. Bubble area is portfolio share, and bubble colour is the Loss Ratio. The chart explains the previous slide’s headline finding. COMP-N is not unprofitable because of one component alone. It is unprofitable because it sits in the upper-right “double trouble” quadrant, where claims happen more often and each claim also costs more. The mechanism makes sense. COMP-N is the no-excess comprehensive product, which removes any out-of-pocket cost to the policyholder. That probably increases the propensity to claim small damages and also removes the deductible’s natural cap on severity. TP, the basic third-party-only cover, sits in the safe quadrant because it caps the insurer’s exposure by design.

title: Insurance PortfolioProfitability & Volatility
text:
Temporal. Diagnosing the Deterioration










Figure 10







The deterioration is a pricing story, not a loss-cost story.

Premium per exposure has fallen 9% over the window. The book is being written for less money per unit of risk.
Pure premium per exposure is net flat (+3%).
Frequency is up 3% and severity is roughly flat.

Conclusion
The 14-point LR climb is overwhelmingly driven by inadequate premium growth, not by claims inflation.
This re-frames the whole remediation playbook, from “tighten claims handling” to “restore pricing discipline”.



For me this is the slide that re-wires the whole study. All five LR components are rebased to 100 in 2022, so the chart reads as “which line is doing the damage”. The visual answer is unambiguous. The red Loss Ratio line is rising because the blue Premium per Exposure line is falling. Claim frequency, severity, and pure premium per exposure are basically flat over the three-year window. There is no claims-inflation crisis on this book. The crisis is in pricing. The insurer is writing 2024 risks for nine percent less premium per unit of exposure than it charged in 2022. This re-frames every conventional remediation impulse. The right answer is not to tighten claims handling, not to invest more in fraud detection, and not to renegotiate supplier panels. It is to restore pricing discipline and re-rate aggressively, especially in the COMP-N segment that just crossed 100 percent in 2024.

Three interaction patterns, three packages
1. Hover and inspect
A plotly heatmap of LR by policy_type x bonus_score, faceted by year. Hover any cell to read the exact LR, exposure and incurred. Toggle the year slider to see the deterioration in motion.

A crosstalk plus plotly scatter (premium vs. incurred) paired with a per-type LR box-plot. Drag a rectangle on the scatter and the box-plot recomputes in real time on just the brushed policies. The “see and discover” loop in one widget.
3. Drill-down
A ggiraph lollipop of LR by top-20 vehicle brands. Hover for tooltip, click to reveal underlying records. Static aesthetics with an interactive payload.










Figure 11








The bonus part of the study demonstrates three interaction patterns, each chosen because it solves a different analytical need. Hover and inspect is for when the reader knows what to look at but needs exact numbers. It turns a colour-encoded heatmap from approximate into precise, without breaking the overall picture. Linked brushing is probably the most useful pattern, because it lets the reader paint a region of the scatter and immediately see the marginal Loss Ratio distribution recompute live, so they can find their own subsets. Drill-down with ggiraph keeps the publication-quality look of a static ggplot figure but layers tooltips and click-to-filter behaviour on top. The static preview on this slide is the brand lollipop. The technical report renders the full interactive version, since revealjs presentations can be heavy when too many widgets are embedded.

text:
Findings and Recommendations


Profitability

Product mix dominates. A 39 pp LR spread, and COMP-N crossed 100% in 2024. Start any remediation here.
Cancelled bleed. 128% LR vs. 64% for Active. Investigate adverse-retention pathways.
Bonus-malus leakage. Neutral (81%) ranks worse than Bad (79%). The classification rule is over-inclusive.
Diesel premium gap. 9 pp hotter than gasoline. A re-rate study is warranted.

Volatility

Tail-risk machine. Gini 0.95. Top 1% of policies = ~50% of losses. Only reinsurance can manage this.
COMP-E carries highest CV. Most volatile within-segment despite only the second-worst mean.



Next steps


GLM Re-rate on validated drivers


Tail Per-risk u/w limits + XoL




Bonus Split Neutral into Neutral-Up and Down


Monitor Quarterly Premium / Exposure KPI


The one-slide takeaway
The 14-point LR climb is a pricing story, not a claims story. Restore pricing discipline, contain the tail with reinsurance, and re-rate COMP-N first.



Six findings on the left, four next steps on the right, structured to flow from diagnosis to action. The first four findings sit on the profitability side, and findings five and six belong to volatility. Each of the four recommendations on the right maps back to at least one finding. A GLM re-rating directly addresses findings one through four. A tail-risk programme addresses finding five. A bonus-class redesign closes the leakage identified in finding three. And a quarterly pricing health monitor would have flagged the 2024 erosion at least six months before it showed up in the loss ratio. The one-slide takeaway in the bottom right is the conclusion the whole deck has been building towards. The headline number, a 14-point Loss Ratio climb, is a pricing problem, not a claims problem. Fixing it from the claims side would be the wrong move.
